Looking for a truly unique Japanese dining experience in Tokyo? 🍣🇯🇵

Ginza Okeya isn’t just a sushi restaurant—it’s an immersive theatrical omakase experience that combines Japanese cuisine, craftsmanship, culture, and live performance.

Created by the team behind Okeya Kyujiro, which has earned Michelin recognition across three cities in Canada, this unique dining concept has now arrived in the heart of Ginza.

The dinner experience features an omakase course of around 25 dishes, prepared with carefully selected seasonal ingredients and served right in front of you.

But what makes this place truly special is the presentation.

From the chefs’ movements and live preparation to the tableware, lighting, sound, and atmosphere, the entire dinner unfolds almost like watching a performance on stage. 🎭🍣

It’s not simply about eating great sushi—you get to experience Japanese craftsmanship and culture through all five senses.

English-speaking staff are also available, making it an especially memorable experience for international travelers looking for something beyond a typical sushi dinner.

Located just a 3-minute walk from Ginza Station, this is one of those dining experiences worth adding to your Tokyo bucket list.

Save this for a special night in Japan! 🇯🇵✨

Little coffee shop run by a single grandma🥹
You can have one of the most local experiences in Tokyo right here in Shibuya. While everyone rushes through the busy streets and famous crossings, this tiny coffee shop feels like a little slice of everyday life hidden in the middle of the city. The owner runs the entire shop by herself and has been in business for over 50 years. There’s even a note on the menu explaining that she prepares everything alone and asking customers to be patient. She was honestly the sweetest. She knows all the neighborhood dogs and locals would regularly stop by just to say hello while she always had dog treats ready for them! I ordered the breakfast set, which came with coffee brewed using a traditional siphon and a piece of toast bigger than my face alongside a boiled egg. It was simple, comforting, and exactly the kind of experience I love finding in Japan. Save this if you’re looking for a slower, more meaningful coffee experience in Tokyo and send it to someone who loves discovering local hidden gems over big chains!

If I could recommend just one restaurant in Kanazawa, it would be this one. Not only is the food incredible, but the solo owner is one of the kindest people I met in Japan. He told me he began learning from his mentor, Ken Okumura, back in 1974. Their specialty has always been steak, and after his mentor passed away, he took it upon himself to continue the restaurant and honor everything he had built. After eating here, I can confidently say you won’t be disappointed. We chatted through a translator, and he shared that he’s also an artist who loves painting and creating intricate origami. Before I left, he surprised me by creating and gifting me a few of his handmade pieces. I was so touched by such a thoughtful gesture! He also told me that international visitors are some of his favorite customers. When I mentioned I was from Canada, he was so excited and thanked me for traveling all the way to Kanazawa. He said lunchtime is usually quiet, so he enjoyed having the chance to chat while preparing the food he loves making. Save this spot if you’re looking for an unforgettable meal in Kanazawa, and send this to someone who’s always choosing local hidden gems over trendy restaurants!

How to avoid Tokyo’s BIGGEST tourist trap ❌

Tsukiji Market is Tokyo’s most popular fish market and also a top must-visit spot for most tourists visiting Japan!  Because of how popular it is, most of their seafood, sushi and sashimi are marked up to tourist prices and it’s extremely expensive. 

If you want to enjoy fresh seafood, sushi and sashimi at prices locals ACTUALLY pay for, head to 📍Tsukiji Uogashi which is just literally next to Tsukiji Market. It consist of 2 buildings that are connected to each other by a bridge. Everything here is way cheaper, and it’s not crowded. 

Enjoy your visit to Tsukiji Uogashi and make sure to try their toro and uni for a fraction of the price 😉

Don’t take the Shinkansen to Kyoto… 

….ride this train instead!

We’ve been on hundreds of trains in Japan and I’m here to tell you this one is by far one of the most special! 

The best part is, it runs between 2 of Japan’s most popular cities - Kyoto and Osaka.

📍 It’s called the Kyo Train Garaku

But you’ll need to plan your trip! It only runs a few times a day and only on weekends and public holidays - that’s how special this train is!

And because we don’t want you to miss out…

✨ HERE’S EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW ✨

⏰ Arrive at least 30 mins early. It’s super popular with locals, and you’ll want to be first in line to grab the best seat

🍱 You can eat & drink on board but honestly, we didn’t see anyone doing this 

🚅 It’s slower than the Shinkansen (45-50 mins vs 15 mins) but soooo much more scenic 

🚫 This little beauty is not covered by the JR Pass, so you’ll need a separate ticket 

🎟️ You don’t need to pre book. Just ride for the regular fare. Tap your IC card or buy a physical ticket

💴 It’s crazy cheap, only $4AUD/$2.80USD to ride, compared to $20 for the Shinkansen 

🚉 In Osaka, the train departs from Osaka-umeda Station

🚉 In Kyoto, catch it from Kyoto-kawaramachi Station 

🪴By gosh the tatami-style floors, zen garden, and beautiful plush seats are to die for!

✨TOP TIP: Board near the front for the best seat by the window or facing forward - you can thank me later!

It’s easy to stick to Tokyo and Kyoto when visiting Japan, but if you’re skipping these underrated gems, you’re only scratching the surface of what this beautiful country has to offer. From coastal villages to hidden temples, here are 10 must-see places in Japan that travelers often miss—but shouldn’t!

1️⃣ Chureito Pagoda – That iconic Mount Fuji view you see on postcards? This is where it’s taken. A must-visit during cherry blossom season.
2️⃣ Adashino Nenbutsu-ji Temple (Kyoto) – Thousands of moss-covered Buddha statues tucked away in the Arashiyama hills. Peaceful, spiritual, and surreal.
3️⃣ Kyushu Island – Hot springs, volcanoes, and incredible food. Japan’s most underrated island.
4️⃣ Nachi Falls – The tallest waterfall in Japan, right next to a vermillion pagoda. A true fairytale view.
5️⃣ Lake Kawaguchiko – One of the best spots for unobstructed views of Mount Fuji, plus relaxing onsen and scenic lakeside walks.
6️⃣ Echizen Daibutsu – One of Japan’s largest Buddha statues, completely overlooked by most tourists. Located in quiet Fukui Prefecture.
7️⃣ Tsubosaka Dera Temple – A hidden temple with sweeping valley views and massive Buddha statues—almost always empty of crowds.
8️⃣ Ine Fishing Village – Nicknamed “the Venice of Japan,” this coastal town is full of boathouses built right on the water. Peaceful and photogenic.
9️⃣ Okinawa & the Kerama Islands – Tropical blue waters, coral reefs, and a whole different side of Japan most people miss.
🔟 Edo Wonderland (Nikko) – A full-blown time-travel experience to the samurai era with live shows, ninja performances, and traditional costumes.

If Japan is on your bucket list, don’t just do the basics—do it right. 😉

This cozy café-restaurant in Nagoya is known for serving the cutest tiramisu!

There has never been a better time to buy a watch in Japan. 

1. Low Prices
Thanks to a number of macroeconomic factors that started in the ‘90s, the Japanese Yen is really low. The watch market has not fully adjusted yet so you are able to find amazing steals. On top of this, in Japan 10% VAT is deducted straight from the price at the shop.

2. Large Vintage Market
Due to its economic prosperity in the ‘80s, Tokyo is the best vintage city in the world. Particularly if you take into consideration Japan’s attitude towards good maintenance. You will be able to find rare and unique pieces in amazing condition.

3. Watch Trends
Japan doesn’t always follow the same trends as the rest of the world as it can be quite trend insular. Popular watches abroad are still unwanted here and priced accordingly.

Most importantly just enjoy your trip and lose yourself in the experience.

2. Upper purchase limit will be removed

This unique monorail ride is one of the many interesting activities you can find in Tenkawa, a mountain village in Nara Prefecture. 

The monorail leads all the way to the hidden Goyomatsu Stalactite Cave, which was discovered by Goyomatsu Akai. Over the ensuing decades, his family poured their resources into its exploration and development. To honor their dedication, the cave was named “Godaimatsu,” and a bronze bust was erected in tribute.

After stepping into a realm of mystery and adventure within the cave, visit the nearby onsen city, Dorogawa Onsen. I’d recommend staying here for at least a night to explore the surrounding countryside!

Perhaps Japan’s cutest train? This is the Tama Densha in Wakayama prefecture. The train has a heartwarming backstory. 

In 2006 the train line was on the verge of bankruptcy when a stray cat named Tama was appointed stationmaster of Kishi Station. Her popularity saved the train line and boosted the local economy. 

Unfortunately Tama passed away in 2016 (with 3,000 attending her funeral 🙀) and there is a small shrine on the platform at Kishi station dedicated to her. 

Nitama and Yontama, her successors, are “working” between 10am and 4pm with 2 days off and rotating schedules.

I understand that the cats are kept behind glass to keep people from touching or grabbing them. It would be great to see them roam the cafe though! Nitama has a decent amount of space but Yontama’s enclosure is much smaller. 

The trains were designed by Eiji Mitooka, one of Japan’s most beloved train designers 🚃

If you’re coming to Japan, save this post and don’t forget to add a car meet to your itinerary 🏎️🇯🇵

Car meets in Tokyo can be an exciting and less popular way to immerse yourself in Japan’s automotive culture. You’ll find all sorts of events, from casual gatherings to more exclusive and private ones, each showcasing a variety of themes from drift cars to vintage models or specific makes and models. I recently attended my first one, and it definitely won’t be my last 😎

I found out about a pop-up event called @theclutchkickback and @tokyomotorcollection at UDX in Akihabara through word of mouth. It was a ticketed event, costing 1000 yen to get in. It was so much fun—the atmosphere was lively with great music, friendly people, and, of course, incredible cars. 

It’s a community event where enthusiasts come together to share their passion, exchange knowledge, and socialize. You get to see the creativity and craftsmanship that owners put into their vehicles up close 🙌🏼

You can expect a diverse range of vehicles, from highly modified drift cars and meticulously restored vintage Japanese classics to the latest high-performance sports cars and luxury imports. Even if cars aren’t your main interest, the setting itself is unique and entertaining.

These kinds of meets and pop-ups happen more often than you might think—all you need to do is a little bit of research! After networking with a few people, I’m already planning to go to a drift event next week. I’m excited to share that experience with you 😬
